content.text: Encoding changes how data is written, and anyone can reverse it. Hashing turns data into a fixed-size fingerprint that can't be turned back, but it can be guessed when the input is predictable. Only encryption keeps data secret, and only as long as the key stays secret. To pick one, ask two questions: do you need the original back, and who must never read it?
A code review flags a column named
. The values look like noise, and many of them end in
. A reviewer copies one into a terminal, runs
, and reads a customer's bank account number. The helper that "encrypts" it is two lines long, and neither of them mentions a key.
The belief: Base64 and hashing are light forms of encryption. The output is unreadable, so the data is protected.

It's an easy mistake, because all three produce output that looks random to a human. They also show up together: keys, ciphertexts and signatures are usually stored and sent as Base64, so Base64 starts to look like part of the security. Hashing is described as "one-way", which sounds like protection. And hashing really does protect something, just not secrecy. The three operations answer different questions, and using one in place of another fails quietly, until someone reads the data.
Encoding changes the format, not who can read it

maps any bytes onto 64 printable characters, so binary data can travel through places built for text: JSON, URLs, email, configuration files. RFC 4648, which defines it, says base encoding is used "to store or transfer data in environments that, perhaps for legacy reasons, are restricted to US-ASCII data." There's no key. The alphabet is published in the RFC, and every language ships a decoder.

The RFC's security section is blunt: "Base encoding visually hides otherwise easily recognized information, such as passwords, but does not provide any computational confidentiality." It adds that this "has been known to cause security incidents", for example when someone shares a network trace to report a bug and reveals a password without realizing it.
Hashing makes a fingerprint, not a secret

takes input of any length and returns a fixed-length digest. MDN lists what makes one fit for cryptography: it must be "one-way: given the output, it should be impractical or impossible to regenerate the original input", any change to the input must change the output, and two inputs with the same output must be impractical to find. SHA-256 always returns 256 bits, written as 64 hex characters.

Two consequences follow. First, you can't get the data back, so a hash is useless for anything you must read later, like an IBAN you pay out to. Second, the same input always gives the same digest. One-way stops anyone from computing backward, but not from guessing forward: if the input is a phone number or an email, an attacker hashes every candidate and compares. Hashing is the right tool for integrity checks, file fingerprints and comparisons. Passwords are a special case that needs a deliberately slow password hash, which a later article in this path covers.
Encryption hides data behind a key

Encryption turns data into ciphertext that only the key holder can turn back. The algorithms are public, so the whole secret is the key. OWASP's Cryptographic Storage Cheat Sheet recommends AES "with a key that's at least 128 bits (ideally 256 bits)" and says authenticated modes such as GCM "should always be used" where available, because they "provide guarantees of the integrity and authenticity of the data, as well as confidentiality." That's
: a changed ciphertext fails to decrypt instead of returning garbage.
. AES-GCM used a random throwaway 256-bit key and a new random nonce each time, and its output (nonce, ciphertext and tag together) is printed as Base64, because ciphertext is bytes too:

rows.text: No, but guessable inputs can be found

content.text: Replacing emails or phone numbers with their SHA-256 in an "anonymized" export doesn't hide them. Anyone with a list of candidates, such as a leaked email list, can hash it and match every row. If the data must stay secret, encrypt it or leave it out.

blocks.title: Lose the keys, lose the data

content.text: Encrypted data is only as durable as its keys. Microsoft warns that "Deleting a key makes its protected data permanently inaccessible", and that in Docker the keys should live in a persistent volume or an external store. Back up the key ring and keep it away from the data, as OWASP advises, so one SQL injection can't expose both.

blocks.title: Spot fake encryption in a review

content.text: method that takes no key isn't encrypting. Another quick check: protect the same value twice. If the outputs are identical, ask why, because modern authenticated encryption adds a random nonce each time.

items.title: Ask two questions per sensitive field

content.text: Do you need the original back? Encrypt it. Do you only need to verify or compare it? Hash it. Neither? OWASP's advice is that "The best way to protect sensitive information is to not store it in the first place."

items.title: Use a vetted library, never your own algorithm

content.text: In ASP.NET Core, Data Protection covers most cases. OWASP's entire guidance on custom algorithms is three words: "Don't do this."

items.title: Store keys apart from the data

content.text: Keep keys in a key vault or a protected key ring, never in source control or in the same database as the ciphertext. Plan rotation and backups before you encrypt the first row.

items.text: Base64 is a format for moving bytes as text; anyone can decode it, and it protects nothing.
A hash is a fixed-size fingerprint: you can't reverse it, but you can guess predictable inputs.
Encryption keeps data secret only while the key stays secret; use authenticated modes like AES-GCM.
Pick by need: read it back means encrypt, compare it means hash, neither means don't store it.
Use a vetted library such as ASP.NET Core Data Protection, and keep keys away from the data.
